# The Dark Is a Country

There is a version of night that almost nobody alive has met.

Not the night of a bedroom with blackout curtains, not the confused first minutes of a power cut, but the whole night: the dark that was, for a hundred thousand years, simply the world after sunset. To meet it now you have to work at it. You drive hours past the last strip mall, into desert or high plains or open water, until the nearest town is a glow on the horizon like a fire over distant hills. Then you stand still and wait, because your eyes are not ready. The human eye needs half an hour or more to build up rhodopsin, the light-catching pigment of its rod cells, and through that wait its sensitivity climbs by thousands of times. What happens at the end of the wait is the strangest ordinary thing on Earth.

The sky thickens. Stars arrive not all at once but in layers, faint ones surfacing behind bright ones like fish rising in a pond, until counting becomes a joke and you give up and stop seeing stars individually at all and start seeing the sky as a single fabric with texture. And then, on a truly dark night, the Milky Way resolves. It is not the pale smudge of photographs. It is a river of light with currents and shoals, dark channels running through it, wide enough that your fist cannot cover it, and it arches over you so completely that you feel less like you are looking up than like you have lain down inside a sphere. Under a bright moon you can read a newspaper headline. Under the Milky Way you can walk. The landscape dims to silver-gray shapes; the sounds sharpen to compensate; and after a while a specific calm arrives, unlike any other calm, the calm of knowing exactly where you are: on a planet, among planets, turning through the edge of a galaxy you can see.

For nearly the whole history of our species, this was not an event. It was an ordinary Tuesday.

Today, by the best estimates, a third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, and most of the rest have to travel to do it. Night, which was once the largest and most reliable thing in the world, has become a destination. I want to make an argument about what we did, and about what it might mean that we did it so casually, without ever quite deciding to.

Night used to be a country. It had borders, laws, an economy, and customs of its own. The very word curfew comes from the French couvre-feu, "cover fire": in medieval towns a bell rang in the evening and households banked their hearths, and the day was formally closed. Roman law held that a thief surprised at night could be lawfully killed, while the same man in daylight could be killed only if he came armed and fought back, because night changed what people were, and made their fear a different kind of reasonable. Night was also ruinously expensive. Artificial light meant fire, and fire meant fuel and danger; by one economic historian's estimate, an hour of lamplight in the ancient world cost something close to a day's wages. So people organized their lives around the moon the way we organize ours around the clock. The Harvest Moon, the full moon nearest the autumn equinox, rises soon after sunset for several nights running, and farmers used those long silver evenings to bring in the crop. Travel, courtship, threshing, and gossip all bent themselves around moonlight. Night had its own physics. It changed distances, changed sounds, changed trust.

It also changed what people did. The old languages are full of the night's one indigenous predator: the "mare" in nightmare was a demon who sat on sleepers' chests, and the suffocating dream was her weight. But night was the domain of story too, and not incidentally. People who worked fields from dawn to dusk had only darkness left over for song, for tales, for courting, for argument. The dark was the first theater and the first church. Monks rose at intervals through it to sing the Night Office. If light meant work, dark meant the rest of being human.

Into that country goes a historian named Roger Ekirch, who in the 1980s began reading his way through the paper trail of pre-industrial nights: diaries, court depositions, medical manuals, sermons, novels, letters. And he kept tripping over a phrase. First sleep. It turns up everywhere once you look for it, more than five hundred times in the records of early modern Europe. Chaucer's Criseyde, sleepless with dread on the eve of her exile, lies awake until her first sleep is somehow behind her anyway. The French had premier sommeil; the Italians, primo sonno. The Psalmist says, "At midnight I will rise to give thanks," and no one for centuries would have found the timing odd.

The pattern they were describing was this. People went to bed not long after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then, quite naturally, woke up. They called the waking interval "the watch." It lasted an hour or two, sometimes more, and it was not insomnia; it was the middle of the night, structurally. People prayed, and many of the old midnight prayers were written precisely for this gap. They tended the fire. They smoked. They talked quietly with family or went over the fence to a neighbor by moonlight. They interpreted their dreams, because a dream from the first sleep arrived on unusually fresh paper, and the first sleep's dreams were widely thought to be the meaningful ones. They made love; a sixteenth-century French physician advised couples that the interval after first sleep was in fact the best time to conceive. Then they went back to bed, into what some sources call the second sleep or morning sleep, and slept until dawn.

For a long time this could be dismissed as a cultural habit, a European quirk of tallow and church bells. Then in the 1990s a sleep researcher named Thomas Wehr ran an experiment. He took volunteers and gave them fourteen hours of darkness every day, for a month, no lamps, no screens, nothing but dark. At first they slept eleven hours a night, paying down a debt none of them knew they carried. And then, by the fourth week, their sleep split. A block of deep sleep. A stretch of quiet, restful wakefulness, during which Wehr noticed the hormone prolactin rising, the same hormone elevated in nursing mothers. Another block of sleep. Given darkness enough, the body reassembled a rhythm that had been discontinued, like a limb falling asleep and then waking with pins and needles. An anthropologist who had worked with the Tiv of Nigeria in an earlier era reported that they still spoke of first and second sleep as natural facts, and found the idea of one long unbroken unconsciousness faintly absurd.

What ended the practice was light. Not instantly, and not Edison alone; gaslight began it, and then the grid finished it, and by the 1920s the phrases first sleep and second sleep had gone strange and archaic, like words for vanished farm tools. Ekirch drew one corollary that deserves to be more famous. What sleep clinics call middle-of-the-night insomnia, the complaint of waking at three and being unable to return to sleep, may in part be the old pattern breaking through the modern expectation of a single continuous sleep. The waking is ancestral. What makes it torment is the panic, the conviction that something is broken, which is exactly the kind of conviction you can only have in a world where nobody has ever heard of the watch. Some sleep therapists now tell their patients the quietly radical thing: lying peacefully awake in the middle of the night is not failure. It is, historically, normal.

But the larger thing that ended was not a sleep schedule. It was a country.

Consider what happened to the price of light. In the ancient world, an hour of lamplight cost a day's wages, by one estimate; today an hour of bright light costs a fraction of a second of an average one. We did not merely buy more light than our ancestors. We bought the abolition of night as an institution, the same way certain technologies abolished distance. Look at the NASA composites, the Earth at night, Europe's coastline drawn in gold thread, and you are looking at a map of wealth and power as legible as any atlas: the Korean peninsula at night shows the south as a constellation and the north as an absence, a darkness with one small spark where Pyongyang is. Light is money and order. Darkness is whatever is left.

And the sky itself has been paying. A landmark study found that more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and that the Milky Way is hidden from three out of five Europeans and roughly four out of five North Americans. Worse, it is getting worse: one recent analysis of citizen observations found the night sky brightening by nearly ten percent a year, a rate at which the stars you can see halve within a decade. The single best anecdote about all this comes from the Northridge earthquake, which struck Los Angeles at 4:30 in the morning in January 1994 and knocked out power across the city. In the sudden dark, residents began calling the police and the Griffith Observatory to report an alarming phenomenon, a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging over the blacked-out hills. It was the Milky Way. People were calling emergency services about their own galaxy, because it had appeared where it had no right to appear, over a city where it had not been visible in living memory.

The cruelty of it is that nobody chose this. Every porch light is rational. Every car dealership's floodlit lot is somebody's livelihood. The abolition of night is a tragedy of the commons written in photons, and it is also, in one narrow sense, the most forgiving pollution on Earth: unlike mercury or carbon, light leaves no residue at all. Turn it off, and the dark comes back complete, as if nothing had ever happened.

Meanwhile the dark was doing more work than we knew. It was not an absence but an instruction. The body reads light at all times; melatonin flows only in darkness; the WHO's cancer agency has classified night-shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen, which is a clinical way of saying that the night shift is an exposure, like asbestos with better lighting. And the dark was habitat. Sea turtle hatchlings orient toward the brighter horizon, which for a hundred million years meant the sea and its reflected sky; today they crawl inland toward the sodium glow of a beachfront road, and volunteers in Florida spend their nights flipping them around. Moths may steer by keeping their backs toward what they take for the sky, which is a sensible navigation trick until the sky is a streetlight and up is down; they spiral in until they die or are eaten, their oldest instinct used against them. Fireflies flash their courtship into a glare that answers nothing. Hundreds of millions of birds die each year colliding with buildings in North America, many drawn off course by the glitter of cities they mistake for something navigable. Even trees are confused; streetlit ones hold their leaves longer, unwilling to accept that summer is over. The dark was a biome. We are demolishing it at the speed of development, and since it belongs to no one, no one is its keeper.

Here is the part I find hardest to get over. You cannot see the stars in daylight. Not because they are gone; they are there at noon exactly as at midnight, pouring across the sky while you eat lunch. Daylight doesn't remove them. It drowns them. Darkness is not the opposite of light but its medium, the one register in which faint things become real. Your eyes know this: in the dark they spend half an hour building their instrument, and then whole galaxies are available. The oldest sky-readers on Earth took the point literally. Aboriginal Australian astronomers chart constellations made not of stars but of darkness itself, the Emu in the Sky drawn in the black dust lanes beside the river of the Milky Way; the Inca saw a llama and a fox in the shadow-clouds between the stars. There are figures you can only see in the dark, and they vanish first.

I would not push the metaphor too far, but I notice that it keeps being true. Most of what matters in a life is faint. Grief is faint. Memory is faint. Other people's inner lives are faint, and so is your own when you finally get quiet enough to hear it. These things show best in unlit hours: the drive home, the long wait, the middle of the night when the whole bright apparatus of the day is switched off and something small and true comes up like a star. We have gotten very good at medicating such hours with feeds and noise, and I include myself, but it is worth being honest about what the treatment costs. A world that is fully lit all the time is a world in which only the bright things are permitted to be real.

None of this is an argument against light. Let me be clear about that, because the temptation to romanticize is strong and the truth is not romantic. Pre-electric night was cold, and frightening, and it killed people: the fever that turned bad overnight, the fire in the thatch, the childbirth with no lamp bright enough to help. Artificial light is one of the plainest, least complicated goods in the entire human story. The surgeon's lamp. The light left on for someone coming home late. The woman reading after her children sleep, the first women in history free to do so. No one should have to live in the old dark. The argument is only against thoughtlessness, against totality, against the assumption that because a little light is good, all light is better.

And there are already people keeping the dark on purpose, the way we keep wilderness. Flagstaff, Arizona, passed the first municipal lighting ordinance in 1958, not out of sentiment but to protect the sky over Lowell Observatory, where Pluto had been found twenty-eight years before; the city has been quarreling gracefully with its own glow ever since. We are the first generations who could give the night away entirely, and therefore the first who have to choose it.
